memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'I will set my face against any Israelite or any foreigner residing among them who eats blood, and I will cut them off from the people.'" - Lev 17:10 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
I will set my face against. That is intensely personal language. God does not say the person will suffer consequences, or that the community will act. He says: I will deal with this Myself.

It is the same phrase used elsewhere for the most serious offences. God is not indifferent to how His people treat what is holy.

We are often uncomfortable with this side of God. We prefer the gentle Shepherd and quietly set aside the God who opposes. But a God incapable of opposition would be a God incapable of love. A father who watched his children destroy themselves with a pleasant smile would not be kind. He would be absent.

The same Jesus who welcomed children made a whip and drove the traders out of the temple (John 2:15). The same Lamb of God is described in Revelation in terms of wrath (Rev 6:16). We do not get to keep half of Him.

And here is the thing: God's opposition is never arbitrary. Notice the next verse will explain exactly why blood mattered so much. He always tells His people why.

The God who sets His face against sin is the God who set His face towards Jerusalem to die for sinners (Luke 9:51).

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Are you comfortable only with the gentle side of God's character?
2. Why is God's opposition to sin an expression of His love?
3. How do God's holiness and His mercy meet at the cross?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, You are holy and You take sin seriously, and I thank You that this is part of Your love. Help me not to shrink You down to something comfortable. Amen.
